input: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 2.02, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and bottoms of 2 mol% light component. The Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 11.1 theoretical stages, the reboiler included, at total reflux. The minimum is a bound, not a design: it is the stage count the separation would need at total reflux, where no product is withdrawn and the reflux ratio is at its largest. The actual design works at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, so the column operates away from the total-reflux condition and needs more stages than the minimum. How many more is not a Fenske result. The stage count at the design reflux comes from a separate simulation, and the Fenske figure stands as the check that simulation is read against. A simulated count below the minimum would contradict the bound, and a count far above it would point to the reflux choice rather than to the separation itself. The constant-volatility assumption runs through both calculations, so the comparison between the bound and the simulation is made on one basis throughout. It also disciplines the reading of the simulation in a second way, because the gap between the simulated count and the minimum is the part of the design attributable to the finite reflux ratio, and that gap, rather than the raw count, is the figure the reflux choice should be judged on. The bound also fixes what the simulation must respect at its own reflux ratio, because no finite-reflux column separates the stated products in fewer stages than the total-reflux minimum.
